claims.claim: ASCL1-high and NEUROD1-high compartments can be clearly identified by sub-clustering the neuroendocrine differentiation group.
claims.source: By sub-clustering the neuroendocrine differentiation group, we could clearly identify ASCL1-high and NEUROD1-high compartments, as well as several other groups of cycling cells that did not cleanly fit into any lung lineage cell identity (Figure 4D, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: Finding from sub-clustering analysis, shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The NE-variant cluster was associated with increased expression of genes highly expressed in variant SCLC (NEUROD1, SCG3, IGFBPL1, SSTR2, and MYC).
claims.source: We conducted differential gene expression to further characterize the NEUROD1-high (abbreviated 'NE-variant') and ASCL1-high (abbreviated 'NE') clusters observed with RPM cells (from cell lines and tumors) and found that the NE-variant cluster was associated with increased expression of genes highly expressed in variant SCLC (NEUROD1, SCG3, IGFBPL1, SSTR2, and MYC) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: Finding from differential gene expression analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The NE (or 'NE-classic') cluster was linked to heightened expression of genes ranging from histones (HISTH1B, HISTH1D) to redox processes (MT1E, MT2A).
claims.source: In contrast, the NE (or 'NE-classic') cluster was linked to heightened expression of a variety of genes ranging from histones (HISTH1B, HISTH1D) to redox processes (MT1E, MT2A) (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: Finding from differential gene expression analysis, shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Gene set enrichment analysis of the NE-variant cluster revealed increased expression of genes associated with activation of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (p=6.81 × 10–3).
claims.source: Gene set enrichment analysis of these results in the NE-variant cluster revealed increased expression of genes associated with activation of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (p=6.81 × 10–3) and pancreatic beta cell signaling (p=1.01 × 10–3).
claims.evidence: Finding from gene set enrichment analysis of differential expression results.

claims.claim: Gene set enrichment analysis of the NE-variant cluster revealed increased expression of genes associated with pancreatic beta cell signaling (p=1.01 × 10–3).
claims.source: Gene set enrichment analysis of these results in the NE-variant cluster revealed increased expression of genes associated with activation of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (p=6.81 × 10–3) and pancreatic beta cell signaling (p=1.01 × 10–3).
claims.evidence: Finding from gene set enrichment analysis of differential expression results.

claims.claim: The NE-variant cluster was linked to lower levels of oxidative phosphorylation (p=1.07 × 10–25).
claims.source: However, this cluster was also linked to lower levels of oxidative phosphorylation (p=1.07 × 10–25), possibly suggesting these subgroups of cells are biologically different (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: Finding from gene set enrichment analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: RPM and RPM (T58A) cells were associated with higher expression of genes associated with cells in dividing phases of the cell cycle than were observed in RP cultures.
claims.source: Further examination of the ASCL1-high and NEUROD1-high clusters revealed that, across both clusters, RPM and RPM (T58A) cells were associated with higher expression of genes associated with cells in dividing phases of the cell cycle than were observed in RP cultures.
claims.evidence: Finding from cell cycle analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: RPM cells were associated with a 10-fold increase in G2M cells in the NE cluster compared to RP cultures (p=9.6 × 10–6).
claims.source: We compared the proportion of G2M cells between culture-derived RPM and RP models. This revealed that RPM cells were associated with a 10- and 11-fold increase in the NE and NE-variant clusters, respectively (NE p=9.6 × 10–6, NE-variant p=1.9 × 10–7) with a relative reduction in cells in the G1 phase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: Statistical finding from cell cycle analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: RPM cells were associated with an 11-fold increase in G2M cells in the NE-variant cluster compared to RP cultures (p=1.9 × 10–7).
claims.source: We compared the proportion of G2M cells between culture-derived RPM and RP models. This revealed that RPM cells were associated with a 10- and 11-fold increase in the NE and NE-variant clusters, respectively (NE p=9.6 × 10–6, NE-variant p=1.9 × 10–7) with a relative reduction in cells in the G1 phase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: Statistical finding from cell cycle analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: The joint density was highest for cells that co-express MYC and NEUROD1 and was localized to the NEUROD1-high cluster.
claims.source: We computed the cellular density of co-expression patterns of cells that express MYC in addition to either ASCL1 or NEUROD1. This identified that the joint density was highest for cells that co-express MYC and NEUROD1 and was localized to the NEUROD1-high cluster (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: Finding from co-expression analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: ASCL1 and MYC expressions are negatively correlated (Pearson r=–0.11, p=1.5 × 10–4).
claims.source: Similar to what was previously reported by other groups, we found that ASCL1 and MYC expressions are negatively correlated (Pearson r=–0.11, p=1.5 × 10–4).
claims.evidence: Statistical correlation analysis from single-cell RNA-seq data, consistent with prior reports.

claims.claim: A modest correlation between MYC and NEUROD1 expression was identified in single-cell data (Pearson r=0.17, p=3.7 × 10–4).
claims.source: Moreover, a modest correlation between MYC and NEUROD1 expression was identified in our single-cell data (Pearson r=0.17, p=3.7 × 10–4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: Statistical correlation analysis from single-cell RNA-seq data, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: An extremely strong correlation between MYC and NEUROD1 expression was identified in bulk primary and metastatic RPM tumors (Pearson r=0.93, p=0.02).
claims.source: Although we couldn't determine co-expression within the same cell using bulk gene expression data, we identified an extremely strong correlation between the expression of these two genes (Pearson r=0.93, p=0.02, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: Statistical correlation analysis from bulk RNA-seq data, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claims.claim: The overexpression of MYC (WT or T58A) may be linked to an SCLC-N phenotype.
claims.source: Taken together, we show that the overexpression of MYC (WT or T58A) may be linked to an SCLC-N phenotype.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the co-expression and correlation analyses.

claims.claim: Enrichment patterns in RPM and RPM (T58A) xenografts revealed that both ASCL1- and NEUROD1-high clusters expressed SCLC-N-associated genes more frequently than SCLC-A and SCLC-P-associated counterparts (p<2.2 × 10–16).
claims.source: Enrichment patterns in RPM and RPM (T58A) xenografts revealed that both ASCL1- and NEUROD1-high clusters expressed SCLC-N-associated genes more frequently than SCLC-A and SCLC-P-associated counterparts (p<2.2 × 10–16, Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: Statistical finding from subtype enrichment score analysis, shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: RP cell cultures more closely resembled cells from tumors with an SCLC-A phenotype (p<2.2 × 10–16).
claims.source: In contrast, RP cell cultures more closely resembled cells from tumors with an SCLC-A phenotype (p<2.2 × 10–16, Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence: Statistical finding from subtype enrichment score analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I.

claims.claim: All RPM xenografts strongly exhibited an SCLC-N transcriptional program.
claims.source: Moreover, we found that all RPM xenografts strongly exhibited an SCLC-N transcriptional program.
claims.evidence: Finding from cellular deconvolution analysis of bulk RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Overexpression of WT or mutant MYC alters the transcriptional identity of RP cells, encouraging neuroendocrine differentiation.
claims.source: Taken together, these data suggest that overexpression of WT or mutant MYC alters the transcriptional identity of RP cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C), encouraging neuroendocrine differentiation, and may assist with the transformation from a SCLC-A to SCLC-N phenotype.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the transcriptional profiling and subtype analyses, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C.

claims.claim: Overexpression of WT or mutant MYC may assist with the transformation from a SCLC-A to SCLC-N phenotype.
claims.source: Taken together, these data suggest that overexpression of WT or mutant MYC alters the transcriptional identity of RP cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C), encouraging neuroendocrine differentiation, and may assist with the transformation from a SCLC-A to SCLC-N phenotype.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the transcriptional profiling and subtype analyses, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C.

claims.claim: The addition of an efficiently expressed transgene encoding normal or mutant human MYC can convert weakly tumorigenic human PNEC cells into highly malignant, metastatic SCLC-like cancers after implantation into the renal capsule of immunodeficient mice.
claims.source: In this report, we show that the addition of an efficiently expressed transgene encoding normal or mutant human MYC can convert weakly tumorigenic human PNEC cells, derived from a human ESC line and depleted of tumor suppressors RB1 and TP53, into highly malignant, metastatic SCLC-like cancers after implantation into the renal capsule of immunodeficient mice.
claims.evidence: Summary of the main finding of the study, supported by all experimental data presented.

claims.claim: SCLC is a highly aggressive cancer with a relatively stereotypic genotype that is generally recalcitrant to therapeutic strategies that have not changed appreciably in the past 30 years.
claims.source: Because SCLC is a highly aggressive cancer with a relatively stereotypic genotype that is generally recalcitrant to therapeutic strategies that have not changed appreciably in the past 30 years, we have been attempting to generate a model for SCLC in which the cancer cells are human in origin, derived from the most commonly affected pulmonary cell lineage (neuroendocrine), and equipped with the major and most common genotypic and phenotypic changes characteristic of SCLC.
claims.evidence: Established knowledge about SCLC characteristics and treatment history.

claims.claim: The choice of MYC to serve as an oncogenic driver in hESC-derived PNECs was based on the frequent finding of high levels of MYC RNA in human SCLC.
claims.source: Our choice of MYC to serve as an oncogenic driver in hESC-derived PNECs was based on both the frequent finding of high levels of MYC RNA in human SCLC and the use of Myc overexpression strategies to generate aggressive mouse models of SCLC (Ireland et al., 2020; Mollaoglu et al., 2017; Huijbers et al., 2014; Ciampricotti et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Rationale for experimental design based on known characteristics of human SCLC and prior mouse models.

claims.claim: The choice of MYC to serve as an oncogenic driver in hESC-derived PNECs was based on the use of Myc overexpression strategies to generate aggressive mouse models of SCLC.
claims.source: Our choice of MYC to serve as an oncogenic driver in hESC-derived PNECs was based on both the frequent finding of high levels of MYC RNA in human SCLC and the use of Myc overexpression strategies to generate aggressive mouse models of SCLC (Ireland et al., 2020; Mollaoglu et al., 2017; Huijbers et al., 2014; Ciampricotti et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Rationale for experimental design based on prior mouse models, supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Not all human SCLC tumors have abundant MYC RNA.
claims.source: However, not all human SCLC tumors have abundant MYC RNA, and other genes, including other members of the MYC gene family, have been implicated in the pathogenesis of SCLC.
claims.evidence: Acknowledgment of heterogeneity in human SCLC, based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: Other genes, including other members of the MYC gene family, have been implicated in the pathogenesis of SCLC.
claims.source: However, not all human SCLC tumors have abundant MYC RNA, and other genes, including other members of the MYC gene family, have been implicated in the pathogenesis of SCLC.
claims.evidence: Established knowledge about genetic drivers of SCLC.

claims.claim: The hESC-derived tumors arising from RPM RUES2 cells belong to the SCLC-N subtype.
claims.source: Transcriptional profiling has also allowed us to conclude that the hESC-derived tumors arising from RPM RUES2 cells belong to the SCLC-N subtype, one of the major subtypes of SCLC now recognized by several laboratories and clinicians studying SCLC.
claims.evidence: Conclusion from transcriptional profiling analysis presented in the study.

claims.claim: It is unclear whether SCLC-N truly represents a subtype of SCLC with distinct outcomes and therapeutic sensitivities, or rather a snapshot from a continuum in tumor evolution driven (principally) by MYC toward an aggressive, recalcitrant disease.
claims.source: It is unclear whether SCLC-N truly represents a subtype of SCLC with distinct outcomes and therapeutic sensitivities (Gay et al., 2021), or rather a snapshot from a continuum in tumor evolution driven (principally) by MYC toward an aggressive, recalcitrant disease (Choudhuri et al., 2023; Pongor et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Discussion of uncertainty in the field, supported by citations to conflicting perspectives.

claims.claim: Metastatic spread was observed from RPM tumors growing initially in the renal capsule but not from primary subcutaneous tumors initiated with the same cell culture.
claims.source: Finally, we note that in the experiments reported here, metastatic spread was observed from RPM tumors growing initially in the renal capsule but not from primary subcutaneous tumors initiated with the same cell culture.
claims.evidence: Summary of experimental observations comparing injection sites.

claims.claim: Metastatic spread may depend on the site(s) of growth of the primary tumor.
claims.source: It may prove important to test other sites of primary tumor growth with RPM cells from the RUES2 line or with other SCLC models, to determine the degree to which metastatic spread depends on the site(s) of growth of the primary tumor and to identify specific factors that promote such spread.
claims.evidence: Speculation about future experiments based on current observations.

results.result: TP53/RB1-deficient hESC-derived PNECs form benign, non-aggressive tumors. The authors previously showed that PNECs with reduced TP53 and RB1 expression form subcutaneous tumors in immunodeficient mice, but these tumors grow slowly without invasion or metastasis, contrasting with human SCLC behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C14, C15, C16, C23, and C24 consistently describe the benign nature of RP tumors across multiple injection sites and experimental conditions. The findings are supported by histological data and prior published work (Chen et al., 2019), with consistent observations in both subcutaneous and renal capsule injections.

results.result: Addition of MYC to TP53/RB1-deficient PNECs produces aggressive, metastatic SCLC-like tumors. Doxycycline-regulated expression of wild-type or mutant MYC (T58A) in RPM cells injected into the renal capsule promotes rapid tumor growth, local invasion, and metastasis primarily to the liver.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C19, C20, C36, C37, C38, and C78 are well-supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D, 3D, and accompanying histological analyses. The quantitative finding that approximately half of DOX-treated animals developed metastases (C37) provides statistical support. The site-specific requirement for metastasis is demonstrated by comparing renal capsule versus subcutaneous injections.

results.result: RPM cells show DOX-inducible knockdown of TP53/RB1 and expression of MYC. Western blot analysis confirms that RPM and RPM(T58A) cells contain dramatically reduced TP53 and RB1 proteins and produce MYC protein after DOX treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C21 and C22 are directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B. The experimental validation is appropriate and clearly demonstrates the expected molecular changes upon DOX induction.

results.result: RPM tumor growth is DOX-dependent and reversible. RPM tumors grow more rapidly than RP tumors, require continuous DOX provision, and can be induced even after delayed DOX administration up to 2 months post-injection.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C29 are supported by tumor growth kinetics data in Figure 2A-B. The DOX withdrawal and add-back experiments provide strong evidence for DOX-dependence. The inference in C29 about cell viability is reasonable given the experimental results, though direct viability measurements are not shown.

results.result: Subcutaneous RPM tumors are histologically consistent with SCLC but do not metastasize. While RPM tumors show SCLC-like histology and rapid growth subcutaneously, they fail to produce metastases to liver or lungs, suggesting microenvironment requirements for metastatic spread.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C33 are supported by histological data in Figure 2C and experimental observations. The inference in C33 about microenvironment requirements is reasonable given the differential metastatic behavior between injection sites, though it remains speculative. The citation support for renal capsule characteristics (C34) is appropriate.

results.result: RPM tumors show increased vascularization and invasion, with metastases retaining primary tumor characteristics. RPM tumors display enhanced vascularization and invasion compared to RP tumors, and metastatic lesions maintain similar proliferative character, MYC expression, and neuroendocrine markers (NCAM, NEUROD1) as primary tumors, while lacking ASCL1 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C35, C40-C43, C45, and C46 are well-supported by immunohistochemical data in Figures 3E-G. The comparative analysis between RP and RPM tumors, and between primary and metastatic sites, is thorough. The inference in C44 about MYC facilitating ASCL1-to-NEUROD1 transition is reasonable given the differential expression patterns, though mechanistic validation is not provided.

results.result: No metastases were observed in bone, brain, or lymph nodes. Histological examination revealed absence of metastatic spread to these organs.
results.evaluation: Claim C39 is a straightforward negative finding from histological examination. While the absence of evidence is noted, the claim is appropriately stated as an observation rather than a definitive conclusion about metastatic potential to these sites.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-seq identifies three major cell populations in differentiated cultures. Integration of RP and RPM single-cell data reveals basal-like (KRT19+), fibroblast-like (COL1A1+), and neuroendocrine (ASCL1+) clusters, with the neuroendocrine cluster expressing ASCL1 and NEUROD1 but not POU2F3.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 are supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A-B. The clustering approach using reference mapping and manual curation is appropriate. The identification of YAP1 expression in non-neuroendocrine cells (C51) is supported by prior literature on hESC cultures.

results.result: MYC overexpression expands the neuroendocrine compartment. RPM cells show 2-3 fold enrichment of neuroendocrine cells compared to RP cells, with specific expression of MYC (not MYCN or MYCL), and EGFP expression strongly correlates with MYC.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C58 are supported by differential cluster abundance analysis and correlation statistics with highly significant p-values (p<2.2×10⁻¹⁶). The specificity for MYC over other family members (C54-C57) is well-documented. However, the analysis accounts for EGFP+ sorting bias, which is appropriate but should be noted as a potential confounding factor.

results.result: Sub-clustering reveals distinct ASCL1-high and NEUROD1-high neuroendocrine populations with different gene expression profiles. The NE-variant (NEUROD1-high) cluster shows increased expression of variant SCLC genes, EMT activation, and pancreatic beta cell signaling genes, but lower oxidative phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 are supported by sub-clustering analysis and differential gene expression shown in Figure 4D-E and supplements. The gene set enrichment analysis provides statistical support (p-values ranging from 10⁻³ to 10⁻²⁵). The biological interpretation of these expression patterns is reasonable, though the functional significance of pancreatic beta cell signaling in SCLC context is unclear.

results.result: RPM cells show increased proliferation compared to RP cells. RPM and RPM(T58A) cells display 10-11 fold increases in G2M phase cells in both NE and NE-variant clusters compared to RP cultures.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 are supported by cell cycle analysis with highly significant p-values (p<10⁻⁶). The findings are consistent across both neuroendocrine subclusters and align with the observed rapid tumor growth phenotype.

results.result: MYC expression correlates with NEUROD1 but not ASCL1. Co-expression analysis shows highest density for MYC+NEUROD1+ cells in the NEUROD1-high cluster, with negative correlation between MYC and ASCL1 (r=-0.11) and positive correlation between MYC and NEUROD1 in both single-cell (r=0.17) and bulk (r=0.93) data.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 are well-supported by correlation analyses with appropriate statistical testing. The extremely strong correlation in bulk data (C71, r=0.93, p=0.02) is notable, though the small sample size (n appears limited) warrants caution. The consistency between single-cell and bulk data strengthens the conclusion. The inference in C72 linking MYC to SCLC-N phenotype is reasonable given the data.

results.result: RPM tumors exhibit SCLC-N transcriptional identity. Enrichment analysis shows RPM xenografts preferentially express SCLC-N-associated genes (p<2.2×10⁻¹⁶), while RP cultures resemble SCLC-A phenotype, and deconvolution analysis confirms all RPM xenografts strongly exhibit SCLC-N transcriptional programs.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C77 are supported by subtype enrichment scoring (Figure 4G) and cellular deconvolution analysis (Figure 4H) with highly significant p-values. The use of published SCLC subtype signatures (Chan et al., 2021; Rudin et al., 2019) for classification is appropriate. The inference about MYC-driven transformation from SCLC-A to SCLC-N (C76-C77) is reasonable but remains correlative rather than mechanistic.

results.result: MYC addition promotes SCLC-N subtype formation. The authors demonstrate that MYC overexpression encourages formation of the SCLC-N subtype marked by high NEUROD1 expression, consistent with findings from other groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C84 are supported by the comprehensive transcriptional profiling data (C73-C77) and are consistent with cited literature. The classification as SCLC-N is well-supported by multiple analytical approaches including enrichment scoring and deconvolution.

results.result: SCLC subtype and NEUROD1 expression are maintained during metastatic spread. RNA-sequencing of paired primary and metastatic samples shows that SCLC subtype does not change upon metastasis and NEUROD1 production is maintained.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C6 are supported by immunohistochemical data (Figure 3E-F) showing comparable NEUROD1 expression in primary and metastatic lesions, and by the strong MYC-NEUROD1 correlation in bulk RNA-seq of paired samples (C71). However, the number of paired samples analyzed appears limited, which should be noted.

results.result: Metastatic spread depends on primary tumor site. The authors observe that metastatic spread occurred from renal capsule tumors but not from subcutaneous tumors, suggesting site-dependence of metastatic potential.
results.evaluation: Claims C86 and C87 are supported by the experimental comparison between injection sites (Figures 1D, 2C, 3D). The observation is clear and reproducible. Claim C87 appropriately frames this as speculation requiring future investigation rather than a definitive mechanistic conclusion.

results.result: Additional oncogenic changes beyond TP53/RB1 loss are required for malignant SCLC. The authors' findings support the hypothesis that full transformation requires additional changes such as MYC family proto-oncogene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C17 and C18 are supported by the experimental comparison between RP and RPM cells, showing that TP53/RB1 loss alone produces benign tumors while addition of MYC produces aggressive, metastatic disease. This is consistent with cited literature on mouse models.

results.result: Background on hESC differentiation and SCLC biology. The authors describe their prior work differentiating hESCs into lung epithelial cells including PNECs, the likely precursor of SCLC, with TP53 and RB1 commonly lost in human SCLC.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 describe established prior work by the authors and general knowledge about SCLC, appropriately supported by citations to their previous publications and the broader literature.

results.result: Historical context on cancer model systems. The authors provide examples of cancer models that lack verisimilitude but have been valuable for understanding carcinogenesis, and note advances in stem cell technology enabling human cell-based cancer models.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 provide appropriate historical and technological context, supported by citations to classic work (Varmus and Weinberg, 1993) and more recent stem cell-derived cancer models (Funato et al., 2014).

results.result: Rationale for model development and MYC selection. The authors justify their approach based on SCLC's aggressive nature, stereotypic genotype, treatment resistance, and the frequent finding of high MYC levels in human SCLC and successful use of MYC in mouse models.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 provide appropriate rationale for the experimental design, supported by established knowledge about SCLC characteristics and multiple citations to prior mouse models using MYC overexpression. The acknowledgment of heterogeneity (C82-C83) is appropriate.

results.result: Uncertainty about SCLC-N as a distinct subtype. The authors note ongoing debate about whether SCLC-N represents a distinct subtype with unique outcomes or a stage in MYC-driven tumor evolution.
results.evaluation: Claim C85 appropriately acknowledges uncertainty in the field and cites conflicting perspectives (Gay et al., 2021; Choudhuri et al., 2023; Pongor et al., 2023). This represents honest discussion of limitations in current understanding.

results.result: MYC overexpression (wild-type or T58A mutant) combined with RB1/TP53 suppression in hESC-derived PNECs produces rapidly growing, invasive, and metastatic SCLC-like tumors when injected into the renal capsule, but not when injected subcutaneously. Metastases occurred primarily in the liver and occasionally in the lung, but not in bone, brain, or lymph nodes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this as the major finding, stating 'the authors provide convincing evidence that RB/TP53 suppression coupled with MYC overexpression in an ES cell-derived model system results in aggressive and metastatic SCLC.' One reviewer notes the limitation that 'subcutaneous tumors don't metastasize, and even with renal capsule models metastases are not common and do not go to important sites (e.g. brain),' but this is acknowledged as a limitation rather than a refutation of the core finding.

results.result: Previous RP models (RB1/TP53 suppression without MYC) produced only small, benign, slow-growing tumors without invasion or metastasis, establishing the baseline that MYC addition improves upon.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as established prior work that contextualizes the current study. One reviewer summarizes: 'the resulting RP xenografts lacked important characteristics of SCLC. Unlike SCLC, these tumors proliferated slowly and did not metastasize.' This is treated as accepted background rather than contested.

results.result: MYC overexpression drives a shift from SCLC-A (ASCL1-high) to SCLC-N (NEUROD1-high) subtype, with RPM tumors expressing NEUROD1 and lacking ASCL1, while RP tumors show the opposite pattern. Single-cell and bulk RNA-seq analyses confirm RPM tumors belong to the SCLC-N subtype.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this finding without challenge. One reviewer notes 'Gene expression analyses revealed that RPM tumor subpopulations expressed NEUROD1, ASCL1 and/or YAP1' and describes the model as showing SCLC-N characteristics. The subtype classification is accepted as a key characterization of the model.

results.result: Paired primary and metastatic tumors maintain the same SCLC subtype and expression of key markers (NEUROD1, NCAM/CD56, MYC) upon metastatic spread, demonstrating phenotypic stability.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these findings about metastatic lesion characteristics. The data on paired samples is presented as part of the accepted characterization of the model's behavior, with no concerns raised about the methodology or conclusions.

results.result: Western blot and RNA-seq analyses confirm that RPM cells express the introduced MYC transgene (not MYCN or MYCL) and have reduced TP53 and RB1 protein levels as designed.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these molecular characterization data without question. These are treated as straightforward validation of the genetic manipulations, with no concerns raised about the western blots or expression analyses shown in the figures.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-seq reveals that RPM cells have expanded neuroendocrine compartments (2-3 fold increase), increased proliferation (10-11 fold more G2M cells), and distinct gene expression patterns including EMT activation, altered metabolism, and strong MYC-NEUROD1 correlation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the single-cell RNA-seq findings or their interpretation. These detailed molecular characterizations are accepted as supporting evidence for the model's properties, with no methodological concerns raised about the computational analyses.

results.result: The authors conclude that full malignant transformation of PNECs requires additional oncogenic changes beyond RB1/TP53 loss, specifically MYC family member overexpression.
results.evaluation: One reviewer explicitly questions whether MYC might render RB1/TP53 loss dispensable, stating 'If a molecular hallmark of SCLC, such as loss of RB1 or TP53, has become dispensable with the addition of cMYC, this information is critically important' and requests experiments testing MYC with various combinations of the other manipulations. This indicates uncertainty about the specific mechanistic requirements and whether all three alterations are truly necessary.

results.result: The choice of MYC as the oncogenic driver was based on its frequent overexpression in human SCLC and successful use in mouse models, though the authors acknowledge not all SCLC tumors have high MYC and other MYC family members are also implicated.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note this as a significant limitation. The editor states 'the impact of the work would have been increased with the inclusion of a broader set of genetic perturbations, such as over-expression of MYCL, to better model major SCLC phenotypes.' Another reviewer mentions the authors declined to test other Myc family members. This indicates the MYC-specific focus is seen as incomplete rather than definitively validated.

results.result: The authors speculate that metastatic spread may depend on the site of primary tumor growth, suggesting the renal capsule microenvironment may be particularly permissive for metastasis.
results.evaluation: One reviewer explicitly critiques this limitation, noting 'their data shows that using their model the subcutaneous tumors don't metastasize, and even with renal capsule models metastases are not common and do not go to important sites (e.g. brain).' The reviewer emphasizes this limits how well the model recapitulates widely metastatic human SCLC, indicating the site-dependence is a recognized weakness rather than a resolved mechanistic insight.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement. Both evaluate claims C1, C2, C14-C16, C23-C24 about benign nature of RP tumors as SUPPORTED. OpenEval cites histological data and prior work; peer reviewers accept this as established background contextualizing the current study.

Strong disagreement. OpenEval finds claims C17-C18 (TP53/RB1 loss alone produces benign tumors while MYC addition produces metastatic disease) SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, explicitly questioning whether MYC might render RB1/TP53 loss dispensable and requesting additional experiments to test necessity of all three alterations.

Agreement with acknowledged limitations. Both evaluate metastasis-related claims (C3, C19-C20, C36-C38, C78) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes site-specific requirement and quantitative data. Peer reviewers affirm this as the major finding but note limitations regarding metastasis frequency and anatomical sites.

Agreement on DOX-dependence. Both find claims C25-C29 about tumor growth kinetics and DOX withdrawal/add-back experiments SUPPORTED. These claims overlap with peer result R1's broader evaluation of the metastatic phenotype as convincingly demonstrated.

Agreement on histological findings. Both find claims C30-C33 about histological characteristics SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the microenvironment inference (C33) is speculative but reasonable; peer reviewers accept these as part of the model characterization.

Disagreement on interpretation. OpenEval finds claims C86-C87 (site-dependence of metastasis) SUPPORTED, appropriately framing C87 as speculation. Peer reviewers rate C87 as UNCERTAIN, explicitly critiquing this as a significant limitation that reduces how well the model recapitulates widely metastatic human SCLC.

Disagreement on completeness. OpenEval finds claims C79-C83 (rationale for MYC overexpression design) SUPPORTED with appropriate citations.
